cards.title: Polynomial bit size of short Stabbing Planes proofs
cards.formal: Historical question, resolved affirmatively: is there a universal polynomial p such that, for every n≥1, every unsatisfiable CNF formula F on n Boolean variables and every Stabbing Planes refutation of F with ℓ tree nodes, F also has a Stabbing Planes refutation of total binary encoding length at most p(n+ℓ)? The original refutation may use integer coefficients of arbitrarily large magnitude. The replacement may change the tree and use more nodes; neither the original depth nor the original queried inequalities must be preserved. Dadush and Tiwari’s 2020 recompilation theorem answers this question.
cards.why: Justifies counting branching nodes as a robust proof-complexity measure for Boolean Stabbing Planes, without hiding an uncontrolled amount of information in coefficients. It also clarifies the relationship between geometric branching and finite, checkable proof encodings.
cards.status_note: Read the original open passage and proof definitions, Dadush–Tiwari Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2 with their certificate and input-size discussion, and the original authors’ March 2023 revision acknowledging the resolution. Matched CNF Boolean relaxation, polynomial versus numerical coefficient bounds, node overhead and leaf certification. Kept the input-length dependence for general rational systems. No polynomial-time-in-node-count conversion or independent proof audit is claimed.

progress.text: The source separates length from encoded size and asks whether every short SP refutation has a polynomial-bit replacement.
CCC publication resolves the coefficient question in Theorem 1.1 and provides certified bit-size bounds in Corollary 1.2.
The original authors’ revised full text explicitly records the resolution and includes the certified-size statement as Proposition 4.

cards.definitions: A CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of literals xᵢ or ¬xᵢ. Repeated literals may be deleted and tautological clauses discarded. Its real relaxation K_F⊆[0,1]ⁿ consists of points satisfying ∑ᵢ∈P xᵢ+∑ⱼ∈N(1−xⱼ)≥1 for each clause with positive-variable set P and negative-variable set N, together with 0≤xᵢ≤1 for every i. Unsatisfiable means K_F∩{0,1}ⁿ is empty; K_F itself may contain fractional points. An SP refutation is a finite rooted full binary tree. At each internal node choose a∈ℤⁿ and b∈ℤ; the two outgoing edges add a·x≥b and a·x≤b−1 respectively. At a leaf, the inequalities of K_F together with the branch inequalities on its root-to-leaf path must be infeasible over ℝ. The discarded open slab b−1<a·x<b has no integer points, which makes the branching sound. Each leaf includes an exact certificate of infeasibility: a finite list of input or path inequalities, written in ≥ form, and nonnegative rational multipliers whose weighted sum is 0≥1. Coefficients and constants are encoded in signed binary; rational multipliers use binary integer numerators and positive denominators. Tree topology, every branch vector and threshold, and the leaf certificates are all charged to proof bit size. Input axioms used at a leaf can be specified by their clause or variable-bound encodings; the entire input formula is not counted anew as part of the proof. The encoding uses no arithmetic circuits or other compressed representations for large integers. Length ℓ counts all tree nodes; internal-node or leaf counts are polynomially equivalent conventions. Depth is the maximum number of edges on a root-to-leaf path and is a separate measure. The same input F and variables must be refuted. The target is existence of a small encoded replacement proof, not a polynomial-time construction measured only in n and ℓ when the original proof itself may require far more bits to read.
cards.answer_criterion: The affirmative resolution is a uniform polynomial bound on the encoded replacement refutation, including rational leaf certificates, for every CNF refutation of length ℓ. The published theorem gives at most O(nℓ) nodes with polynomial-bit branch coefficients for K_F⊆[0,1]ⁿ, and the accompanying certificate analysis supplies a polynomial total size. For arbitrary rational input systems, the certified-size bound must also account for the input system’s encoding length. A small bit length must not be confused with polynomially bounded numerical coefficient magnitude.

cards.title: Sum-of-squares automatability on the Boolean cube
cards.formal: Historical question, resolved negatively: does adding all Boolean equalities x_i²=1 guarantee that a degree-d sum-of-squares certificate can be found in time polynomial in the size N of its explicit semidefinite program, whenever such a certificate exists, even if an additive error tending to zero is allowed? More precisely, is there a uniform algorithm A, a polynomial P and a rational error schedule η(N)≥0 with η(N)→0, such that on every promised input with a degree-d certificate of p(x)≥θ, A outputs within P(N) steps an explicit degree-d certificate of p(x)≥θ−η(N)? There is no such universal algorithm: the required output can have superpolynomial bit length, already when d=2.
cards.why: Identifies a concrete limit on translating low algebraic proof degree into algorithmic efficiency. The resolution explains why coefficient encoding and output size must accompany degree bounds in claims about semidefinite optimization.
cards.status_note: Read the source’s exact output question and Boolean extension, the resolving Theorem 2 and Sections 5.1–5.2, and the 2025 follow-up’s distinction between certificate output and decision. Matched the Boolean encoding, degree, explicit bit representation and approximate objective. No complexity assumption is needed for this output-length obstruction; proofs were not independently audited.

cards.definitions:
An input consists of n real indeterminates, rational polynomials p,q₁,…,q_m, a rational threshold θ and an integer degree bound d≥2. The intended feasible set satisfies q_j(x)≥0 and x_i²=1 for all i. Coefficients and exponents are explicitly written in binary. The source already asks the question for quadratic input polynomials, m=O(n), and integer coefficients of polynomial magnitude; the negative example fits these bounded-input conventions after a constant affine change of Boolean variables and clearing constant denominators. The intended feasible set is therefore a subset of {−1,1}ⁿ, possibly with additional constraints.

A degree-d certificate for p≥t is a polynomial identity p−t=σ₀+∑_j σ_j q_j+∑_i λ_i(x)(x_i²−1), where each σ_j is a sum of squares of real polynomials, each λ_i is an arbitrary real polynomial, and every summand on the right has degree at most d. Additional input equalities r=0 can be encoded as r≥0 and −r≥0; allowing arbitrary polynomial multipliers for those equalities is an at-least-as-strong certificate convention, and the published lower bound holds even with that convention. For degree two and quadratic equalities the multipliers are constants, so the conventions coincide.

The explicit semidefinite formulation uses coefficient matching in the monomial basis and positive semidefinite Gram matrices: σ=zᵀGz for a vector z of monomials and a symmetric matrix G with vᵀGv≥0 for every real vector v. N is the binary length of this explicitly constructed rational SDP, including the objective threshold and all coefficient-matching constraints. With the stated small input polynomials it has size n^{O(d)}. Running time is ordinary bit complexity, not a real-arithmetic operation count. The output must explicitly list finite binary rational coefficients of the Gram matrices and equality multipliers, satisfying the exact polynomial identity for the weakened threshold. The additive slack concerns the certified objective bound; arbitrary residual errors in the identity do not qualify. An arithmetic circuit or symbolic exponent tower standing for enormous coefficients is not the explicit certificate requested by the source.

The promise is existence of a degree-d certificate for the original threshold. The algorithm may behave arbitrarily on unpromised inputs. The error schedule is one fixed computable rational function of N, shared by all inputs, with limit zero as N→∞; the polynomial running-time bound is also universal. The negative conclusion is stronger than needed for this formulation: Section 5 supplies a family for which a fixed small positive additive slack still leaves coefficients requiring exponentially many bits. Thus no choice of vanishing error rate rescues the universal output algorithm.

The later counterexample uses Boolean variables w∈{0,1}. The substitution w=(x+1)/2 converts its constraints to the source’s {−1,1} convention, preserves degree, and changes bounded-degree coefficient bit lengths by polynomial overhead. With v variables, the family has degree-two certificates but requires doubly exponentially large coefficients throughout degrees up to a constant multiple of √v. Section 5.2 applies to a polynomial ε−∑_j w_{1j}+k for any fixed ε<1/2. Choosing, for example, an original ε=1/8 leaves the same obstruction after any eventual additive slack at most 1/8. This matches the source’s approximate-certification question as well as exact certification.
cards.answer_criterion: The published negative answer supplies small-input Boolean systems admitting degree-two certificates whose explicit low-degree certificates need superpolynomially many bits, even after a fixed small weakening of the objective. This excludes any polynomial-time output procedure with a vanishing additive error schedule. It does not by itself settle the decision problem of whether such a certificate exists, or a model allowing succinct arithmetic-circuit encodings of coefficients.

context_blocks.title: Booleanity alone is insufficient

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.
